books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: James K. Polk, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, December 5, 1848

stimulus.source_note: James K. Polk, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, December 5, 1848. Public domain.
stimulus.text: The accounts of the abundance of gold in that territory are of such an extraordinary character as would scarcely command belief were they not corroborated by the authentic reports of officers in the public service, who have visited the mineral district, and derived the facts which they detail from personal observation.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from James K. Polk, Fourth Annual Message to Congress, December 5, 1848, public domain
stem: Polk's message is best understood as an attempt to

options.text: warn Congress that the gold reports were exaggerated.
options.misconception: Polk says the reports are corroborated by officers who saw the gold themselves; he confirms them, not warns against them.

options.text: ask Congress to ban migration to California.
options.misconception: Polk confirms the gold and welcomes the news; he does not ask to ban migration.

options.text: confirm the gold reports with official evidence.
claim the gold fields for the federal government.
options.misconception: Polk reports on the gold; he does not claim the fields as federal property.

rationales.A: Polk says the accounts “would scarcely command belief” without corroboration — then gives the corroboration, so he confirms rather than warns.
rationales.B: Polk welcomes the news of gold; nothing in the message asks Congress to stop migration.
rationales.C: Polk cites “the authentic reports of officers in the public service” who saw the gold district themselves — official eyewitness evidence meant to make an unbelievable story believable.
rationales.D: The message reports the gold; it makes no claim that the federal government owns the fields.
rationales.general:
1. Hear Polk's problem. The gold stories were “of such an extraordinary character as would scarcely command belief.”
2. See his solution. He cites officers who visited the mineral district and reported from “personal observation.”
3. Name the move. A president lending official eyewitnesses to a wild story turns rumor into news.
Remember: when a president quotes his own officers, he is borrowing their eyes. The question is why he needs them — here, because the story sounded too good to be true.
